tier_reason: khvzak/script-bench-rs publishes the harness (benches/roto.rs, benches/mlua_lua55.rs, benches/rquickjs.rs, src/*.rs, scripts/sort_userdata.{roto,lua,js}, bench.py), Cargo.toml [profile.bench] opt-level=3, lto=fat, codegen-units=1, rustc v1.99.0 and Apple M5 Max in the README Environment table; the chart 'Sort Rust objects.png' shows roto 12.04 ms vs mlua_lua55 15.47 ms and rquickjs 36.38 ms.

corrections.caveats: Single benchmark (Sort Rust objects: build 10,000 random 8-23 char strings as Rust userdata, then an in-script quicksort calling a Rust comparison), dominated by script-to-Rust interop rather than pure interpreter speed. Numbers exist only in the chart image 'Sort Rust objects.png' (criterion typical estimate, sample_size 10), not as text. Per-language scripts are hand-written ports and not identical: the Roto script was tuned by the Roto maintainer (script-bench-rs PRs #17 'remove some conversions from the Roto script' and #18 'make list swap a native function'), so Roto swaps list elements through a native Rust function while Lua and JS swap in-script; the Roto charset is 15 characters ('9' missing) against 16 in the Lua/JS scripts. Lua 5.5 is the mlua vendored build and QuickJS is reached through rquickjs, not standalone C Lua or QuickJS. Roto is slower than Luau (11.82 ms), Wasmi (7.04 ms) and Wasmtime (2.71 ms) in the same chart. Apple M5 Max only. The Roto README makes no performance claim; the shootout is by the mlua author (independent of Roto, MIT-licensed since July 2026, results refreshed 2026-10-03).

notes: Chart numbers match the record exactly (12.04 / 15.47 / 36.38 ms; 1.28x and 3.02x derived from page data). Harness validates the sorted output for each engine, so no no-op timing; main flaw is that the Roto script was optimized by its own maintainer (native list swap) while the other ports were not, plus the narrow single-workload scope. Metadata checked: BSD-3-Clause, 558 stars, GitHub mirror of codeberg.org/NLnetLabs/roto, last commit 2026-09-22.

tier_reason: First-party harness (ozanh/ugobenchfib cmd/bench/main.go, code/) with Go 1.18 and an Apple M1 VM stated, but it falls short of A: each engine is timed once as a whole process with errors ignored (`_ = cmd.Run()`), go.mod pins ugo v0.1.2 while the table is for 0.2.0-rc (installed by unpinned `go install`), and the native Lua version is unstated.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Go 1.18 (also Go 1.17 tables); engines installed with default `go install` (Makefile setup), no flags; native Lua and Python versions unstated
corrections.caveats: Not faster than the category baseline: native Lua runs fib(35) in 1.000147 s against uGO's 1.984686 s (about 2x faster), and on fibt(35) uGO (1.261 ms) is slower than Tengo (1.135 ms), go-lua (1.006 ms) and native Lua (463 us); the win is only over other Go-embedded engines (Tengo, go-lua, GopherLua, goja). Harness flaws: cmd/bench/main.go times one wall-clock run per engine of the whole process (startup, parse and compile included), ignores the exit status (`_ = cmd.Run()`) and never checks the printed result, so fibt rows in the 1 ms range are mostly process startup. go.mod pins github.com/ozanh/ugo v0.1.2 while the table reports uGO 0.2.0 release candidate, so the measured build is not reproducible from the repo. Run inside a Parallels VM on an Apple M1 host. Numbers date from 2022-05-03; the project is now at v0.5.0 (May 2025).

notes: Numbers in the record match the 2022-05-03 Go 1.18 table exactly. Downgraded A to C for the single-run, error-ignoring process-timing harness and the unpinned 0.2.0-rc build; it also loses to native Lua (category baseline), so it is a Go-ecosystem data point only. Metadata checked: MIT, 125 stars, last commit 2025-05-10 (v0.5.0), stale.

tier_reason: The harness is public (bench/comparison.js, bench/comparison_jsc.zig, bench/comparison_zig_js.zig) with Zig 0.17.0-dev.1441, ReleaseFast and Apple M3 Pro stated, but the baseline's execution configuration is not: comparison_jsc.zig sets no JSC options and records no tier data. JSC's per-operation costs derived from the report (about 15.5 ns per arithmetic iteration, 26.7 ns per fib call) look like its interpreter/baseline tiers rather than DFG/FTL. A first-party claim against a possibly unoptimized baseline is capped at C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README headline: zig-js / JSC throughput 2.32x for a single warmed context (10 of 10 workloads), 2.53x at 8 independent steady contexts, 2.52x at 8 cold lifecycles. The report itself gives JSC single-context throughput as 0.43x zig-js by geometric mean (2.32x recomputed from the medians, derived from page data) and 0.40x at 8 lanes. Per-row JSC/zig-js ranges from 0.19x (fibonacci: 93.659 ms vs 500.404 ms) to 0.82x (object_churn: 109.545 ms vs 132.953 ms).
corrections.caveats: The report says the ten kernels 'deliberately exercise guarded native/VM tiers that zig-js currently implements' and is 'not a claim about applications or unsupported workloads'. The JSC runner (bench/comparison_jsc.zig) calls JSGlobalContextCreate/JSEvaluateScript with no JSC options, and the docs say the public C API exposes no tier counters. Derived from page data, JSC spends about 15.5 ns per iteration of a modulo-add loop (24M iterations in 371 ms) and about 26.7 ns per recursive call (18.76M calls in 500 ms), where zig-js spends 3.6 ns and 5.0 ns. Those JSC costs look like its LLInt/baseline tiers, so its optimizing JIT may not have run in this embedding (unverified; a WebSearch snippet only says JSC disables its JIT for third-party in-process embedders on Apple platforms). The README's own JSON/JIT diagnostic shows system JSC 4.05x faster, and the Wasm SIMD report shows JSC about 10x faster. docs/benchmarks.md 'Latest JavaScriptCore comparison' cites a different July 29 report (commit 0f8b33c: 2.29x/2.51x/2.61x, 9 of 10 wins at 8 lanes) than the README's precise-nursery report (commit 14d94ec). README diagnostics name an Apple M2 Pro while the headline report names an M3 Pro. No CPU pinning. No QuickJS, Duktape or Lua comparison. Very new project (31 stars, about 4,800 commits) with daily changes.

notes: Headline numbers are on the README and match the report's medians (geomean 2.32x recomputed). Downgraded A to C because the baseline may be JSC without its optimizing JIT: the runner sets no JSC options, and JSC's derived per-op costs are interpreter-like. If a JIT-on JSC run (or JSC_useJIT logging) confirms the numbers, this can return to A. Metadata checked: MIT, 31 stars, not a fork, last commit 2026-10-06.
